input.newString:
## Authoring DSL (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`)

- **SwiftUI-shaped builders**: `Text`, `Image`, `Icon`, `Color`, `Rectangle`,
  `Circle`, `Ellipse`, `Capsule`, `RoundedRectangle`, `Shape`, `Divider`, `Spacer`,
  `ProgressView`, `Gauge`, `Label`, `Group`.
- **Containers**: `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `GridRow`, `ScrollView`,
  `LazyVStack`, `LazyHStack`, `LazyVGrid`, `LazyHGrid`, `ViewThatFits`/`Fit`,
  `ProxyView`, `ForEach`.
- **Controls**: `Button` (title or label subtree), `TextField`, `SecureField`,
  `TextEditor`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`, `DatePicker`, `Picker`, `Menu`,
  `ColorPicker`.
- **Automatic child collection**: `VStack { Text("a"); Text("b") }` needs no
  `.children(...)`. A custom `Component` constructed inline in a block
  auto-registers; a view stored as a field is added explicitly with `+field`.
- **Signals**: `signal`, `computed`, `constant`, `effect`, `untracked`,
  `Signal<T>.value`, `WritableSignal<T>.value`, `Signal<T>.map`, `readonly`.
- **Modifier sugar**: `.padding`, `.frame`, `.offset`, `.position`, `.fixedSize`,
  layout priority/z-index/aspect ratio, the full text-formatting surface,
  foreground/background/border/corner radius/shadow, visual effects, transforms,
  visibility/disabled/hit-testing, accessibility, tap/pointer events,
  environment binding, styles, window metadata, and navigation intents.
- **Persisted state**: `Component` base class + `val count by state(0)`
  (auto-keyed by property name) or `state(0, "key")`; a `mutableState(0)` signal
  form for two-way controls.
- **Reactive bodies**: plain `if`/`when`/`for` in `body()`; `ForEach` over a static
  list or `Signal<List<T>>` with row-scoped child collection.
- **Navigation**: `navigator { route(...) }`, `NavigationStack`, `NavigationLink`,
  `isActive`, and `.navigate`/`.push`/`.replace` intents.
- **Media**: `Video(controller)` stays where the app places it; audio remains
  view-less. `controller.register()` projects a controller at the root.
- **Naming**: the composite base is `Component` (renamed from `KotlinView` now
  that the Java DSL is gone); see #174.
- **Java hosting**: a Java Spring Boot / Quarkus app mounts a Kotlin view through
  the Java-friendly `PathlandApp` functional interface
  (`return () -> MusicPlayerView.make();`). Kotlin roots expose public
  constructors and/or `@JvmStatic make(...)` factories.

## Package boundary

- `pathland-view-core` is one Maven module: `core`/`engine`/`dsl` are logical
  subpackages inside it, with a few deliberate intra-module references
  (`Color`/`MediaController`/`Modified` materialize `PathlandNode`). Splitting
  them into separate artifacts would require a node SPI first.
- Production runtimes/renderers (`pathland-server-core`,
  `pathland-render-html`) depend on this module. Framework starters remain
  DSL-neutral at compile time; they mount Kotlin-authored fixture views in test
  scope.

The Java deploy runs on **Maven 3.9.9** (pinned in the workflow): Maven 3.10
writes a `maven-metadata-local.xml` beside each artifact in the Central staging,
which the Portal rejects ("content that does NOT have a .pom file"). The demos
are **excluded from the release reactor** (`-pl '!pathland-demo-common,!pathland-demo-views-kotlin,!pathland-gtk-demo,!pathland-qt-demo,!pathland-quarkus-demo,!pathland-quarkus-kotlin-demo,!pathland-spring-boot-demo'`)

`maven.deploy.skip`, and the demos must not be published.

The publish steps are **idempotent**: a crate+version already on crates.io is
skipped, so re-running a partially failed release is safe (re-run the workflow
via `workflow_dispatch`, passing the `tag`). Maven Central rejects a re-deploy of
an existing version, so a Java re-run only helps if the Java deploy did not
complete.

- **Only changes are sent.** A screen that isn't changing transmits zero bytes.
  Updates are tiny binary deltas, not re-rendered pages or JSON trees.
- **Native elements, not a canvas.** The platform lays out and animates real
  elements — you get native layout, text rendering, and accessibility for free,
  whether those elements are DOM nodes or GTK widgets.
- **A thin client.** The web client is a small static file that hydrates the server
  HTML and applies updates in place. No framework, no virtual DOM, no re-render cost.

## The part you don't write

The web client is a single prebuilt JavaScript file you copy into your static
resources. It's shipped, not maintained — all the real logic lives in your backend.
(There's also a native GTK renderer for desktop.)

## Where it runs today

- **Web (SSR + live WebSocket deltas)** — Kotlin views with Java or Kotlin hosts,
  via the Spring Boot and Quarkus extensions and demos; the flagship getting-started path.
- **Native desktop (GTK4 + Qt)** — renderers driven by the same protocol, from the
  Rust DSL and the shared Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` (`pathland-gtk-demo`,
  `pathland-qt-demo`).

Two surfaces, one protocol — the demos' shared views run under both without a
rewrite.

The SSR path above is the on-ramp — the protocol isn't limited to it.

  delivered through a side-channel callback — they flow through the opcode engine.
  The demo mounts the Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` (the same shared view the web demos use) with the
  app-driven media contract: the renderer plays the tracks through a direct GStreamer
  `playbin` and reports `MEDIA_*` events back; the demo's web-style
  `/_pathland/assets/...` paths resolve against an extracted local asset root
  (`pathland_gtk_set_asset_root`).

The renderer maps native inputs onto the raw `Event` surface via GTK4
controllers (`Button::clicked` → pointer up, `EventControllerMotion` →
pointer move/enter/leave), emitting events through the same `Pump::send_input`
path.

`pathland_gtk::run` passes an explicit empty argv to GTK (the process command
line belongs to the embedding host — e.g. the JVM's `-cp`/`-D` flags — and must
not be parsed as GTK options).

### Kotlin JVM authoring DSL (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`, in `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin`)

The **sole JVM authoring surface**. It is the SwiftUI-like DSL shared by desktop,
Spring Boot, Quarkus, and web apps. Components and modifiers:

- `View` is an **open Kotlin interface** — the library ships `Text`/`Image`/`Color`/
  `Rectangle`, `VStack`/`HStack`/`ZStack`, `Spacer`, `Button`,
  `TextField(placeholder, WritableSignal<String>)`, `Video` (a
  `MediaController`'s surface), and application code defines its own views by
  extending `Component` or implementing `View`. **Media is a state object, not a
  view** (spec/MEDIA.md): `MediaController` owns the resource + transport as

Done on branch `refactor/consolidate-maven-modules`.

**19 → 10 Maven modules**
- `pathland-view-core` absorbs `pathland-view-kotlin`
- `pathland-server-core` absorbs `pathland-state-redis`, `pathland-observability`, `pathland-test-kit`
- `pathland-quarkus` absorbs `pathland-quarkus-kotlin`; `pathland-quarkus-deployment` absorbs `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-deployment`
- `pathland-demo-views-kotlin` absorbs `pathland-demo-common`
- `pathland-desktop-demo` merges the GTK + Qt demos (shared `RingEventReader`)
- `pathland-quarkus-demo` absorbs the Kotlin demo as a mounted `/kotlin` app

Also updated root/CI/release configs, scripts, docs, `AGENTS.md`, and merged/deleted the affected `status.md` files.

**Verification**
- `cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-render-html` — ok
- `cd lib/java && mvn -q -B clean install` — success; all surefire suites green (view-core 61, server-core 71, render-html 12, demos/starter/quarkus ok)
- Quarkus demo shows both `pathland` and `pathland-kotlin` features installed
- Repo-wide grep finds no references to the removed artifact IDs

Changes are staged but **not committed**.

# Pathland Primitive Views

**Wire protocol version:** 1
**Status:** Draft
**Last Updated:** October 15, 2026

---

## Introduction

This document is the **semantic catalog of primitive nodes** the Pathland
protocol supports, organized by the three structural categories that drive
rendering. The **server** (the application/engine) dictates *what* the UI is —
structure, content, and intent. The **client platform renderer** measures
layout geometry, handles font/image assets, and maps each node onto that
platform's native elements, delegating interaction to native OS controls
wherever possible.

Every primitive maps to a protocol component type (`TREE::CREATE_NODE`), the
modifiers that shape it ([MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md)), and the core events it
can produce ([EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md)). This file is **implementation-ready**: a
renderer (GTK, HTML/SSR, or a new backend) can be written from
these tables alone. The wire encoding rules live in
[OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md); this file does not repeat them.

### Structural categories

The protocol splits all supported nodes into three structural categories (the
component ID ranges are definitive — see [Definitive Opcode
Mapping Range](#definitive-opcode-mapping-range)):

| Range | Category | Behavior |
|-------|----------|----------|
| `0x01`–`0x0F` | **Primitive Drawing Nodes** | Low-level, non-decomposable building blocks (`Text`, `Image`, `Color`, `Shape`, `Divider`, `Spacer`, `ProgressView`, `Gauge`). The server dictates exact visual content and structural properties. The client measures layout geometry, handles font/image assets, and paints native elements. They hold **no independent interaction state machines**. |
| `0x10`–`0x1F` | **Layout & Container Primitives** | Structural arrangement (`VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `ScrollView`, lazy grids/stacks). They arrange children and own scroll/virtualization; they carry no interaction semantics beyond scrolling. |
| `0x20`–`0x2F` | **Semantic Control Nodes** | High-order interaction and input controls (`Button`, `TextField`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`, `Picker`, `DatePicker`, `ColorPicker`, `Menu`). They encapsulate intent, two-way bindings (`BINDING_ID`), accessibility traits, and local interaction physics (e.g. 120 FPS client-side thumb dragging). |

### Relationship to other specs

| File | Role |
|------|------|
| [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md) | Wire format: categories, commands, 16-byte opcode layout, ring/arena, value types |
| **PRIMITIVES.md** (this file) | Which **views/nodes** exist and their protocol IDs |
| [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md) | Which **modifiers** (protocol properties) exist and how they encode |
| [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md) | Which **core events** (raw inputs) exist and how they encode |
| [PROXY.md](./PROXY.md) | How a **proxy view** composes a subtree served by another Pathland server |
| [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md) | Golden byte vectors |

> **Implementation status** is tracked per implementing project (a `status.md`
> in each protocol crate/library — `pathland-core`, `pathland-render-gtk`,
> `pathland-render-html`, the Java libraries), **not** in
> this specification. This document defines the protocol contract only.

> **Enum-valued properties** (marked `ENUM` in the tables below) are carried on
> the wire with the `F32` value type, holding the numeric enum code as an f32
> bit pattern (see [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md#value-types)). The codes are listed
> in [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md#appendix-enumerated-values).

### Non-negotiables (recap)

- Views are **declarative structure + constraint properties**, never positions.
  The engine emits `WHAT` (VStack, HStack, Text, …), never `WHERE`.
- Renderers are **stateless**: they map the opcode stream onto native elements
  and lay those elements out with their native layout engine. A renderer MAY
  retain its rendered-output tree for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing —
  this is a cache of its own output, not application state.
- **Native elements everywhere**: each primitive maps to the platform's native
  element (a stack → the platform's native stack; text → the platform's native
  text element); semantic controls → native OS controls in Native Token Mode
  (below). Never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.

---

## Architectural Rules

### 1. Core Structural Classification

Each node belongs to exactly one of the three categories above. The category
determines renderer responsibilities:

- **Primitive Drawing Nodes** hold no interaction state. The server sends the
  full visual description; the renderer measures and paints. If a primitive has
  no native equivalent (e.g. `Path`), the renderer may paint it directly — this
  is the one case where canvas-style painting is permitted.
- **Semantic Control Nodes** carry intent + two-way bindings (`BINDING_ID`),
  accessibility traits, and local interaction physics. Their *visual chrome* is
  delegated per the Dual-Mode rules below; their *interaction semantics* are
  always renderer-owned and reported as raw events.

### 2. Dual-Mode Rendering Pipeline & Platform Delegation

Every semantic control node renders in **one of two modes**, decided by whether
the node has a child layout tree:

#### Native Token Mode (Leaf Control)

When a semantic control node has **no child layout tree** (`childrenIds` is
empty), the client platform **MUST delegate rendering entirely to its native OS
control** — `Button`, `TextField`/`SecureField`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`,
`DatePicker`, `ColorPicker`, `Picker`, and `Menu` each map to the platform's
native control (the concrete widget per renderer lives in that renderer's
`status.md`).

**System style modifiers act as visual style tokens** — they force the platform
to switch native control variants **without emitting child nodes over the
wire**. Example: `TOGGLE_STYLE = CHECKBOX` renders `Toggle` (0x24) as a native
checkbox; `TOGGLE_STYLE = SWITCH` (default) as a native switch; `TOGGLE_STYLE =
BUTTON` as a toggle button.

#### Composite Override Mode (Container Control)

When a semantic control **contains child nodes** (or a custom style body is
defined on the server), the client platform **MUST**:

1. **Suppress** its default native control visuals (the OS control chrome).
2. **Render the custom view tree** sent by the server (the composite body).
3. **Wrap that layout tree** with the native touch/click gestures, focus
   states, and event handlers that give the control its semantics.

The control keeps its interaction semantics (events, two-way bindings,
accessibility) even though its chrome is custom. Example: a `Button` with an
`HStack` child (icon + text) renders the `HStack` and wraps it with a native
click/press gesture that emits the button's events.

#### Leaf Property Fallbacks

If a control (e.g. `Button` 0x20) arrives with an **empty `childrenIds` list**,
renderers **MUST** check for direct string properties (the node's text content
set via `SET_TEXT`, or the `LABEL` 0x200A property for controls that define one)
before falling back to rendering an empty platform control shell. An empty shell
is a last resort, never the primary path.

### 3. Transport-Aware Event Guards

Renderers **MUST** implement event guards to prevent network noise. User
interactions — taps, text changes, drags, value edits — **MUST NEVER** emit
outbound event opcodes unless the target node explicitly declared intent:

- it set the relevant `EVENT_LISTENERS` (0x2005) bits, **or**
- it is a value-bearing control reporting by component type (see

## 5.7 Styleable controls (the style contract)

A **style** customizes a view or control's *content*; the control owns its
*component and interaction*. This is one contract for every styleable surface
(`ButtonStyle`, `LabelStyle`, `VideoStyle`, …), and it is the
author-facing shape of the protocol's **Composite Override Mode**
([PRIMITIVES.md §2](./PRIMITIVES.md#2-dual-mode-rendering-pipeline--platform-delegation)).

- **The control owns the native component and the interaction.** A semantic
  control renders its **native control node** (its component id — `BUTTON`,
  `VIDEO`, …) and attaches its behavior to *that* node: the tap action /
  `EVENT_LISTENERS` (Button), the value/text/date sink, or the media binding
  (`Video`). The **whole control is interactive**, including its padding.
- **The style owns the content.** A style returns the control's **content view**
  from `makeBody(Config)`; the control attaches it as the control node's
  **single child**. The content keeps its own component(s), layout, and
  properties — a style **never** sets or overwrites the control's component and
  never wires the interaction. The result is a control with children → protocol
  **Composite Override Mode**.
- **The style consumes the control's config.** The `Config` a style's
  `makeBody(Config)` receives is the **same type** the view configured through
  `make(...)` ([§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)): `ButtonStyle.makeBody(Button.Config)`,
  `LabelStyle.makeBody(Label.Config)`,
  `VideoStyle.makeBody(VideoStyle.Configuration)`. The style **reads** the config (the
  control's values: content, action, label, media state); it does not mutate it.

## 1. Design principles (DSL-flavored)

These recap the protocol's non-negotiables in author-facing terms. A conformant
DSL must be *shaped* by them:

- **Declarative structure, never positions.** The DSL expresses `WHAT` — a
  `VStack`, a `HStack`, a `Text` — and constraint properties (spacing, padding,
  alignment, size hints). It never computes bounds and never emits rects.
- **Exactly three authoring operations.** Views expose the same three
  operations — **configure values** (§5.0 `make`, §2), **apply modifiers**
  (`modifiers`), and, for content-bearing views, **supply children**
  (`children`). The three are a single fluent builder: any of them may be the
  first call and they may be chained in **any order** (see
  [§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)); a later call overrides an earlier
  value for the same property.

  subtree in `body()`; a signal read there subscribes that **component**, and a
  later write re-renders only that component and diffs its retained subtree.
  The wire still carries only actual changes (`SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY`/
  `SET_DATE`/`TREE`), never a rebuilt tree. A signal **bound** to a node
  (rather than read in `body()`) stays fine-grained: it emits one delta without
  re-running the body. Non-signal reads are mount-time only. The render body
  must be pure/idempotent and must not write signals. This is the
  **per-component reactive body** ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-reactive-bodies--slots)).

  type.** Any modifier applies to any view (`.padding` works on a `Text` and a
  `VStack` alike), and any developer can **author a custom modifier in
  application code** (a `ViewModifier`) that applies to any existing view —
  library primitive, container, control, custom view, or an already-modified
  view (see [§5.6](#56-custom-modifiers-developer-authored)). A modifier a
  given renderer cannot apply is **allowed and ignored** — the property is
  still emitted.

  **not** a separate syntax: they are `ViewModifier` values the library ships,
  composed into a view through the shared `modifiers(...)` operation. There is
  **no per-modifier sugar on the view type** — `Padding` applied via

  modifiers share the same surface.

Because "rich" views like `Button` are **protocol primitives, not DSL compositions** — and that distinction is deliberate.

## The rule

`pathland-engine::Component` is the wire-level node vocabulary (`lib/rust/crates/pathland-engine/src/node.rs:165`). The DSL is the authoring layer that constructs those nodes. Some views map 1:1 to a protocol node; others are pure compositions of existing nodes.

From `spec/PRIMITIVES.md`:
- `0x01–0x0F` primitive drawing (`Text`, `Image`, `Color`, `Shape`, …)
- `0x10–0x1F` layout/container (`VStack`, `HStack`, …)
- `0x20–0x2F` **semantic controls** (`Button`, `TextField`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Picker`, …)
- Composite views (`Label`, `List`, `NavigationStack`) get **no component ID** and are composed in the DSL (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md:225-238`)

So `Button` is intentionally in the third group.

## Why `Button` is not composed from DSL views

If `Button` were just `HStack { Image; Text }.onTap { … }`, the node would be a generic container with a tap handler. It would lose:

- the native control identity (`BUTTON` 0x20 → `GtkButton` at `pathland-render-gtk/src/lib.rs:1877`, `<button>` in HTML at `pathland-render-html/src/lib.rs:1602`)
- renderer-owned focus/pressed/disabled states
- native accessibility/role semantics
- `ACTION_ID` / `EVENT_LISTENERS` / `BINDING_ID` conventions
- the single-node opcode footprint (composition would create extra `TREE` nodes)

That is exactly why `PRIMITIVES.md:110` defines **Composite Override Mode**: a `Button` may have a child subtree supplied by a `ButtonStyle`, but the node remains `BUTTON` and keeps the native interaction semantics (`spec/DSL.md:1026-1045`).

## The DSL still defines `Button`

It is not bypassing the DSL — it is the DSL's primitive constructor:

- Kotlin: `Button.kt:17` → `coreView(Components.BUTTON) { … }`
- Rust: `lib.rs:2728` → `impl View for Button` builds `Component::Button { label }`

`coreView` is the DSL's low-level "make this protocol node" helper. In contrast, `Label` (`Label.kt:17`) really is composed from `HStack` + `Image`/`Icon` + `Text`, because it has no protocol identity.

## Why not use `Component.body()` for `Button`

`Component` is the reactive composite base: a signal read in `body()` subscribes that slot and diffs its retained subtree. `Button` is not a reactive slot — it is a native control node. Making it a `Component` body would force it to be expressed only in terms of other primitives, which is precisely what the protocol design avoids.

## Bottom line

There is no missing DSL abstraction: **semantic controls are primitives by design; only composite views are built from the DSL.** If the concern is consistency, the useful change is documentation/naming (make the primitive-vs-composite rule explicit in `spec/DSL.md`, and perhaps rename `coreView` to something like `primitive`/`leaf`), not composing `Button` etc. If you want, I can plan that docs/naming cleanup.
Kotlin has a DslMarker that helps with scope. Should we use that anywhere?

content.text:
`@DslMarker` only affects **implicit receiver** scopes. The view DSL doesn't use receiver-based builder lambdas — it uses `() -> Unit` plus a thread-local child stack — so the annotation currently does nothing.

## Current state

`Scope.kt:10-13` declares:

```kotlin
@DslMarker
annotation class PathlandDsl
```

…but `@PathlandDsl` is applied to **nothing** (repo-wide grep: only the declaration). The actual child collection is `collectChildren(content: () -> Unit)` at `Scope.kt:67`. So there is no implicit receiver for `@DslMarker` to restrict. It's dead code today.

## Where a scope receiver does exist

Only the receiver-based config/builders:

- `navigator { … }` → `Navigation.Builder.() -> Unit` (`Navigation.kt:21`, builder at `core/router/Navigation.kt:38`)
- `.padding { … }`, `.frame { … }`, `.border { … }`, `.shadow { … }`, `.clipShape { … }`, `.windowMetadata { … }`, `borderedButtonStyle { … }`
  (`Modifiers.kt:83,127,189,221,261`, `Styles.kt:18`, `core/WindowMetadata.kt:15`)

## The real leak `@DslMarker` would fix

Because view-builder lambdas have no receiver, an outer `Navigation.Builder` stays implicitly visible inside them. This compiles today:

```kotlin
navigator("/") {
    route("/") {
        VStack {
            Text("home")
            fallback(Text("oops"))   // resolves to Navigation.Builder.fallback!
        }
    }
}
```

There's a version of this pattern in `DslTest.kt:251`. A `@DslMarker` annotation on a **view-scope receiver** plus `Navigation.Builder` would make that call a compile error. Marking `Navigation.Builder` alone does nothing, because the inner lambda has no annotated receiver to shadow it.

The config builders also share member names (`color`, `width`, `radius`, `padding`, `title`), so marking them is cheap insurance against accidental cross-config calls.

## Options

**A. Remove the dead annotation** (cleanup, no behavior change)
- Delete `PathlandDsl` from `Scope.kt`.
- Docs currently claim it marks entry points; it doesn't.

**B. Minimal marking (cheap, partial)**
- Move the marker to `dev.pathland.view.core` (so `core/router/Navigation.Builder` can use it without a core→dsl package cycle).
- Annotate `Navigation.Builder` + the `*.Config` receiver classes.
- No view-builder signatures change. Protects inside config/router lambdas only; the `VStack { fallback(...) }` leak above remains.

**C. Full scope isolation (recommended if you want the guard)**
- Keep/move a `@PathlandDsl` marker, add an empty `ViewScope` receiver.
- Change builder lambdas from `() -> Unit` to `ViewScope.() -> Unit` (`collectChildren`, `rowView`, all containers, `Button` content, `Label` icon, `Picker`/`Menu` options, `NavigationLink` content, `Fit`, `ForEach` rows).
- Annotate `ViewScope`, `Navigation.Builder`, and all config receivers with `@PathlandDsl`.
- Existing `{ … }` call sites stay source-compatible; only `this`-dependent lambdas would change. Needs a full `pathland-view-core` + reactor test run.

`@DslMarker` is compile-time only — the thread-local `ViewScopes` stack and auto-registration stay exactly as they are.

Which way do you want to go?

options.description: Add a ViewScope receiver to builder lambdas and mark ViewScope, Navigation.Builder and config receivers with @PathlandDsl. Fixes outer-receiver leaks like fallback() inside VStack.

options.label: Minimal marking
options.description: Move the marker to core and annotate Navigation.Builder plus the Config receivers only. No lambda signature changes; partial protection.

options.label: Remove the dead annotation
options.description: Delete the unused PathlandDsl annotation and its misleading KDoc; revisit when real scope receivers are introduced.

## Plan: full Kotlin DSL scope isolation with `@DslMarker`

### Design

- Move the marker to `dev.pathland.view.core` so core receiver types (`Navigation.Builder`, `WindowMetadata.Config`) can use it without a `core → dsl` package dependency.
- Add an empty `PathlandScope` receiver to every view-builder lambda. This gives the compiler an annotated inner receiver, which is what lets `@DslMarker` hide outer DSL receivers.
- Annotate all existing receiver scopes with the same marker.
- The runtime child-collection mechanism (`ViewScopes`, thread-local stack) is unchanged — `@DslMarker` is compile-time only.

### 1. Marker relocation

Create `lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/core/PathlandDsl.kt`:

```kotlin
package dev.pathland.view.core

@DslMarker
@Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS, AnnotationTarget.TYPEALIAS)
@Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY)
annotation class PathlandDsl
```

Remove the unused `@DslMarker annotation class PathlandDsl` and its KDoc from `dsl/Scope.kt`.

### 2. Add the view scope

In `dsl/Scope.kt`:

```kotlin
@PathlandDsl
object PathlandScope
```

Change:

```kotlin
fun collectChildren(content: () -> Unit): List<View>
internal fun rowView(content: () -> Unit): View
```

to:

```kotlin
fun collectChildren(content: PathlandScope.() -> Unit): List<View>
internal fun rowView(content: PathlandScope.() -> Unit): View
```

Invoke with `PathlandScope.content()` inside the existing push/pop block.

### 3. Change builder lambda signatures

In `Containers.kt`:
- `childrenOf`, `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `GridRow`, `ScrollView`, `LazyVStack`, `LazyHStack`, `LazyVGrid`, `LazyHGrid`, `Fit`, `ViewThatFits`
- `content: () -> Unit` → `content: PathlandScope.() -> Unit`

In `Views.kt`:
- `Group`, `Picker`, `Menu`: `content` → `PathlandScope.() -> Unit`
- `ForEach` both overloads: `(T, Int) -> Unit` → `PathlandScope.(T, Int) -> Unit` (call as `content(item, index)` inside the row scope)

In `Button.kt`:
- The two content-bearing overloads: `content: () -> Unit` → `PathlandScope.() -> Unit`
- Leave `action: () -> Unit` unchanged (a callback, not a builder)

In `Label.kt`:
- `icon: () -> Unit` → `icon: PathlandScope.() -> Unit`

In `Navigation.kt`:
- `NavigationLink(to, router, content)` → `content: PathlandScope.() -> Unit`

Callbacks not changed: `onTapGesture`, `effect`, `Button` action overloads.

Existing `{ … }` call sites remain source-compatible. The only break is if someone passes a pre-built `() -> Unit` variable to a builder — none exist in the repo.

### 4. Annotate receiver scopes

Apply `@PathlandDsl` to:

- `PathlandScope` (dsl)
- `Navigation.Builder` (`core/router/Navigation.kt`)
- `WindowMetadata.Config` (`core/WindowMetadata.kt`)
- `Padding.Config`, `Frame.Config`, `Border.Config`, `Shadow.Config`, `ClipShape.Config` (`dsl/Modifiers.kt`)
- `BorderedButtonStyle.Config` (`dsl/Styles.kt`)

Not needed now: `EnvironmentBinding/PointerEvents/PathChange/TapGesture/FontWidth/FontFamily.Config` use `Consumer<Config>` rather than Kotlin receiver lambdas (e.g. `EnvironmentBinding.with { c -> … }`). If receiver-based overloads are added later, mark those too.

### 5. Verification

- `cd lib/java && mvn -q -pl pathland-view-core -am test` — existing DSL tests (including `navigationBuildsAndSwapsDestinations`, `navigationLinkUsesTheNearestRouter`, nested child collection, `ForEach`, `Fit`).
- `cd lib/java && mvn -q -B test` — full reactor, because the builder signatures are public and used by demo views/fixtures.
- Manually confirm the guard in the IDE or a throwaway compile: this should now fail to compile because `fallback` resolves only to `Navigation.Builder`:

  ```kotlin
  navigator("/") {
      route("/") {
          VStack {
              Text("home")
              fallback(Text("oops")) // unresolved inside PathlandScope
          }
      }
  }
  ```

- Existing nested usage (`navigator { route("/") { VStack { … } } }`) must still compile.

### 6. Docs/status

- Update `PathlandDsl` and `PathlandScope` KDoc to explain the compile-time scope guard.
- Update `lib/java/pathland-view-core/status.md` with a bullet under the authoring DSL: `@PathlandDsl` marks view/navigation/config scopes; outer DSL receivers are not visible inside nested view builders.
- No protocol/spec change needed — this is a Kotlin authoring-surface detail.

### Risks

- `PathlandScope` as a public receiver type is a small additive API.
- Hiding the outer `Navigation.Builder` may expose accidental cross-scope calls in application code; that is the intended effect, and the repo currently has none.
- `ForEach`’s receiver + parameter lambda is the one signature worth testing explicitly (`mvn -pl pathland-view-core test`).

protocol-manifest tests; Kotlin DSL tests exercise the emitter end-to-end, and
  the server/HTML/desktop consumers cover their integration paths.

## Authoring DSL (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`)

- **SwiftUI-shaped builders**: `Text`, `Image`, `Icon`, `Color`, `Rectangle`,
  `Circle`, `Ellipse`, `Capsule`, `RoundedRectangle`, `Shape`, `Divider`, `Spacer`,
  `ProgressView`, `Gauge`, `Label`, `Group`.
- **Containers**: `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `GridRow`, `ScrollView`,
  `LazyVStack`, `LazyHStack`, `LazyVGrid`, `LazyHGrid`, `ViewThatFits`/`Fit`,
  `ProxyView`, `ForEach`.
- **Controls**: `Button` (title or label subtree), `TextField`, `SecureField`,
  `TextEditor`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`, `DatePicker`, `Picker`, `Menu`,
  `ColorPicker`.
- **Automatic child collection**: `VStack { Text("a"); Text("b") }` needs no
  `.children(...)`. A custom `Component` constructed inline in a block
  auto-registers; a view stored as a field is added explicitly with `+field`.
- **Signals**: `signal`, `computed`, `constant`, `effect`, `untracked`,
  `Signal<T>.value`, `WritableSignal<T>.value`, `Signal<T>.map`, `readonly`.
- **Modifier sugar**: `.padding`, `.frame`, `.offset`, `.position`, `.fixedSize`,
  layout priority/z-index/aspect ratio, the full text-formatting surface,
  foreground/background/border/corner radius/shadow, visual effects, transforms,
  visibility/disabled/hit-testing, accessibility, tap/pointer events,
  environment binding, styles, window metadata, and navigation intents.
- **Persisted state**: `Component` base class + `val count by state(0)`
  (auto-keyed by property name) or `state(0, "key")`; a `mutableState(0)` signal
  form for two-way controls.
- **Reactive bodies**: plain `if`/`when`/`for` in `body()`; `ForEach` over a static
  list or `Signal<List<T>>` with row-scoped child collection.
- **Navigation**: `navigator { route(...) }`, `NavigationStack`, `NavigationLink`,
  `isActive`, and `.navigate`/`.push`/`.replace` intents.
- **Media**: `Video(controller)` stays where the app places it; audio remains
  view-less. `controller.register()` projects a controller at the root.
- **Naming**: the composite base is `Component` (renamed from `KotlinView` now
  that the Java DSL is gone); see #174.
- **Java hosting**: a Java Spring Boot / Quarkus app mounts a Kotlin view through
  the Java-friendly `PathlandApp` functional interface
  (`return () -> MusicPlayerView.make();`). Kotlin roots expose public
  constructors and/or `@JvmStatic make(...)` factories.

  `View body()`; a signal read there subscribes that component, and a later write
  re-renders only that component and diffs its retained subtree. A signal bound
  to a node stays fine-grained and does not re-run the body. Plain
  `if`/`when`/`for` works; `ForEach` is the reactive list component.

  `Button("Save") { … }`, `.padding`, `.frame`, `.fontSize`, `.background`,

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Multi-stage image for the Pathland Quarkus SSR demo (server-side HTML + /ws deltas).
# Build context is the repository root — the renderer jar embeds the Rust cdylib and
# the demo module needs the Java reactor sources:
#
#   docker build -f lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile -t pathland-quarkus-demo .
#
# See docs/DEPLOY.md.

# --- Stage 1: the Rust HTML renderer cdylib (embedded into the Java jar) ---
FROM rust:1-slim AS rust
WORKDIR /src
COPY lib/rust ./lib/rust
RUN cargo build --manifest-path lib/rust/Cargo.toml -p pathland-render-html

# --- Stage 2: the Java reactor + the Quarkus app (the renderer jar embeds the dylib) ---
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS java
WORKDIR /src
COPY --from=rust /src/lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_render_html.so \
     lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_render_html.so
COPY lib/java ./lib/java
RUN mvn -q -B -f lib/java/pom.xml -pl pathland-quarkus-demo -am package -Dmaven.test.skip=true

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Multi-stage image for the Pathland Quarkus SSR demo (server-side HTML + /ws deltas).
# Build context is the repository root — the renderer jar embeds the Rust cdylib and
# the demo module needs the Java reactor sources:
#
#   docker build -f lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile -t pathland-quarkus-demo .
#
# See docs/DEPLOY.md.

# --- Stage 1: the Rust HTML renderer cdylib (embedded into the Java jar) ---
FROM rust:1-slim AS rust
WORKDIR /src
COPY lib/rust ./lib/rust
RUN cargo build --manifest-path lib/rust/Cargo.toml -p pathland-render-html

# --- Stage 2: the Java reactor + the Quarkus app (the renderer jar embeds the dylib) ---
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS java
WORKDIR /src
COPY --from=rust /src/lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_render_html.so \
     lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_render_html.so
COPY lib/java ./lib/java
RUN mvn -q -B -f lib/java/pom.xml -pl pathland-quarkus-demo -am package -Dmaven.test.skip=true

# --- Stage 3: runtime (JRE only) ---
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=java /src/lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/target/quarkus-app/ /app/
EXPOSE 8080
ENV QUARKUS_HTTP_PORT=8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-Xms64m", "-Xmx256m", "-jar", "/app/quarkus-run.jar"]

## Diagnosis

The failure is in the **Docker build selection**, not the consolidated POMs:

`lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile:22` runs:

```bash
mvn -f lib/java/pom.xml -pl pathland-quarkus-demo -am package -Dmaven.test.skip=true
```

`-am` builds the demo plus its Maven dependencies. `pathland-quarkus-deployment` is **not** a Maven dependency of the demo or of `pathland-quarkus` — it is only named in the runtime's generated `quarkus-extension.properties` as `deployment-artifact`.

When the `quarkus-extension-maven-plugin:extension-descriptor` goal runs on `pathland-quarkus`, it validates the extension by resolving `dev.pathland:pathland-quarkus-deployment:0.1.5` and walking its dependency graph. With the deployment module outside the reactor and a fresh Render container (`~/.m2` has no `dev.pathland` artifacts), the collected deployment graph is empty, so every expected runtime/deployment dependency is reported missing — including `dev.pathland:pathland-quarkus` itself and the new `quarkus-kotlin-deployment`.

Locally and in CI this is masked because both run the **full reactor** (`mvn ... test`), where `pathland-quarkus-deployment` is a reactor project. The Docker command is the only place that excludes it.

## Proposed fix

**Primary change — `lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile`**

Include the deployment module in the selected reactor:

```dockerfile
RUN mvn -q -B -f lib/java/pom.xml \
    -pl pathland-quarkus-demo,pathland-quarkus-deployment \
    -am package -Dmaven.test.skip=true
```

Same behavior for the unsuffixed fallback: build the whole reactor (`mvn -q -B -f lib/java/pom.xml package -Dmaven.test.skip=true`) — proven by the local `mvn clean install`, but slower because it packages every demo.

**CI guard — `.github/workflows/ci.yml`**

After the existing full-reactor `mvn -q -B test` (line 195), add a deploy-path step using the same Maven selection as the Dockerfile, so this cannot regress unnoticed:

```yaml
- name: Package the deployable Quarkus demo
  working-directory: lib/java
  run: mvn -q -B -pl pathland-quarkus-demo,pathland-quarkus-deployment -am package -Dmaven.test.skip=true
```

**Docs — `docs/DEPLOY.md`**

Add a short note that the image build must include `pathland-quarkus-deployment` in the Maven reactor (the runtime's extension descriptor validates against it).

**Do not** make `skipExtensionValidation=true` the primary fix. It would hide a useful check; keep it only as a documented emergency escape hatch (`-DskipExtensionValidation=true`) if the reactor fix ever proves insufficient.

## Verification

1. `cd lib/java && mvn -q -B -pl pathland-quarkus-demo,pathland-quarkus-deployment -am clean package -Dmaven.test.skip=true`
2. Emulate Render's empty local repo (optional but definitive):
   `mvn -Dmaven.repo.local=/tmp/fresh-m2 ...` or just the real Docker build.
3. `docker build --no-cache -f lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile -t pathland-quarkus-demo .`
4. Confirm the image starts and serves SSR + `/ws`.

Do you want me to apply the targeted `-pl ... ,pathland-quarkus-deployment` fix plus the CI guard, or use the full-reactor build command instead?
deployment and ci guard

# Deploying the Quarkus SSR demo

Runs the [Pathland Quarkus demo](pathland-quarkus-demo/) (server-side HTML at any
path + live `/ws` deltas) as a container — the application evidence for the Restack
proposal (issue #71, `docs/PREAPPLICATION-TODO.md`).

The image is multi-stage: it builds the Rust HTML renderer cdylib, embeds it into
the Java `pathland-render-html` jar (which the demo depends on), packages the
Quarkus app, and runs it on a JRE 17 runtime.

## Build

From the repository root (build context must be the root — the embed step needs
the Rust dylib and the Java reactor sources):

```bash
docker build -f lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile -t pathland-quarkus-demo .
```

## Run locally

```bash
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 pathland-quarkus-demo
# → http://localhost:8080
```

A quick check that it serves:

```bash
curl -I http://localhost:8080/          # 200, text/html
curl http://localhost:8080/ | grep -o 'data-pathland-id'   # hydrated SSR markup
```

State defaults to the in-memory store (no Redis needed for the demo). To use
Redis, pass a `REDIS_URL` and the Redis `StateStore` in `pathland-server-core` is
selected at runtime — the standalone demo runs without it.

## Push to a registry

```bash
docker tag pathland-quarkus-demo ghcr.io/<org>/pathland-quarkus-demo:latest
docker push ghcr.io/<org>/pathland-quarkus-demo:latest
```

## Deploy to a host

Any platform that runs a Docker container exposing TCP 8080 works:

- **Railway / Fly.io** — point at the image (or use a Dockerfile deploy); set the
  public port to **8080**. The app binds `0.0.0.0` (see
  `application.properties`).
- **Hetzner / any VPS** — `docker run -d -p 8080:8080 --name pathland pathland-quarkus-demo`
  (optionally behind Caddy/nginx; forward `GET /` and the WebSocket `Upgrade`).
- **Platform port override** — the app honors `QUARKUS_HTTP_PORT` if a platform
  assigns a different port.
